In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **binomial series** is a generalization of the [binomial formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_formula) to cases where the [exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponent) is not a positive integer:

         ( 1 + x  )  α      =  ∑  k = 0   ∞       (   α k   )     x  k         = 1 + α x +    α ( α − 1 )   2 !     x  2   +    α ( α − 1 ) ( α − 2 )   3 !     x  3   + ⋯       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}(1+x)^{\alpha }&=\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }\!{\binom {\alpha }{k}}x^{k}\\&=1+\alpha x+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha -1)}{2!}}x^{2}+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha -1)(\alpha -2)}{3!}}x^{3}+\cdots \end{aligned}}}    1

where     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   is any [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number), and the [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series) on the right-hand side is expressed in terms of the [(generalized) binomial coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient#Generalization_and_connection_to_the_binomial_series)

        (   α k   )    =    α ( α − 1 ) ( α − 2 ) ⋯ ( α − k + 1 )   k !    .   {\displaystyle {\binom {\alpha }{k}}={\frac {\alpha (\alpha -1)(\alpha -2)\cdots (\alpha -k+1)}{k!}}.}

The binomial series is the [MacLaurin series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacLaurin_series) for the [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics))     f ( x ) = ( 1 + x  )  α     {\displaystyle f(x)=(1+x)^{\alpha }}  . It converges when      |  x  |  < 1   {\displaystyle |x|<1}  .

If α is a nonnegative [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) n then the *x**n* + 1 term and all later terms in the series are 0, since each contains a factor of (*n* − *n*). In this case, the series is a finite polynomial, equivalent to the binomial formula.

## Convergence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=1)]

### Conditions for convergence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=2)]

Whether (**[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_1)**) [converges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_series) depends on the values of the complex numbers α and x. More precisely:

1. If |*x*| < 1, the series converges [absolutely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_convergence) for any complex number α.
2. If |*x*| = 1, the series converges absolutely [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) either Re(*α*) > 0 or *α* = 0, where Re(*α*) denotes the [real part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) of α.
3. If |*x*| = 1 and *x* ≠ −1, the series converges if and only if Re(*α*) > −1.
4. If *x* = −1, the series converges if and only if either Re(*α*) > 0 or *α* = 0.
5. If |*x*| > 1, the series [diverges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series) except when α is a non-negative integer, in which case the series is a finite sum.

In particular, if α is not a non-negative integer, the situation at the boundary of the [disk of convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_of_convergence), |*x*| = 1, is summarized as follows:

- If Re(*α*) > 0, the series converges absolutely.
- If −1 < Re(*α*) ≤ 0, the series converges [conditionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_convergence) if *x* ≠ −1 and diverges if *x* = −1.
- If Re(*α*) ≤ −1, the series diverges.

### Identities to be used in the proof

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=3)]

The following hold for any complex number α:

        (   α 0   )     = 1 ,   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose 0}\!=1,}          (   α  k + 1    )     =     (   α k   )       α − k   k + 1    ,   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k+1}\!=\!{\alpha \choose k}{\frac {\alpha -k}{k+1}},}    2        (   α  k − 1    )     +     (   α k   )     =     (    α + 1  k   )    .   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k-1}\!+\!{\alpha \choose k}\!=\!{\alpha +1 \choose k}.}    3

Unless     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   is a nonnegative integer (in which case the binomial coefficients vanish as     k   {\displaystyle k}   is larger than     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  ), a useful [asymptotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_analysis) relationship for the binomial coefficients is, in [Landau notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_notation):

        (   α k   )     =    ( − 1  )  k     Γ ( − α )  k  1 + α       ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) ,   as   k → ∞ .   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k}\!={\frac {(-1)^{k}}{\Gamma (-\alpha )k^{1+\alpha }}}\,(1+o(1)),\quad {\text{as }}k\to \infty .}    4

This is essentially equivalent to Euler's definition of the [Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function):

     Γ ( z ) =  lim  k → ∞      k !   k  z     z ( z + 1 ) ⋯ ( z + k )    ,   {\displaystyle \Gamma (z)=\lim _{k\to \infty }{\frac {k!\,k^{z}}{z(z+1)\cdots (z+k)}},}

and implies immediately the coarser bounds

       m  k  1 + Re  α     ≤  |    (   α k   )    |  ≤   M  k  1 + Re ⁡ α     ,   {\displaystyle {\frac {m}{k^{1+\operatorname {Re} \,\alpha }}}\leq \left|{\alpha \choose k}\right|\leq {\frac {M}{k^{1+\operatorname {Re} \alpha }}},}    5

for some positive constants m and M .

Formula (**[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_2)**) for the generalized binomial coefficient can be rewritten as

        (   α k   )     =  ∏  j = 1   k     (     α + 1  j   − 1  )  .   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k}\!=\prod _{j=1}^{k}\!\left({\frac {\alpha +1}{j}}-1\right).}    6

### Proof

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=4)]

To prove (i) and (v), apply the [ratio test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio_test) and use formula (**[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_2)**) above to show that whenever     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   is not a nonnegative integer, the [radius of convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_of_convergence) is exactly 1. Part (ii) follows from formula (**[5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_5)**), by comparison with the [p-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests#p-series_test)

      ∑  k = 1   ∞     1  k  p     ,   {\displaystyle \sum _{k=1}^{\infty }{\frac {1}{k^{p}}},}

with     p = 1 + Re ⁡ ( α )   {\displaystyle p=1+\operatorname {Re} (\alpha )}  . To prove (iii), first use formula (**[3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_3)**) to obtain

     ( 1 + x )  ∑  k = 0   n       (   α k   )     x  k   =  ∑  k = 0   n       (    α + 1  k   )     x  k   +    (   α n   )     x  n + 1   ,   {\displaystyle (1+x)\sum _{k=0}^{n}\!{\alpha \choose k}x^{k}=\sum _{k=0}^{n}\!{\alpha +1 \choose k}x^{k}+{\alpha \choose n}x^{n+1},}    7

and then use (ii) and formula (**[5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_5)**) again to prove convergence of the right-hand side when     Re ⁡ ( α ) > − 1   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )>-1}   is assumed. On the other hand, the series does not converge if      |  x  |  = 1   {\displaystyle |x|=1}   and     Re ⁡ ( α ) ≤ − 1   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )\leq -1}  , again by formula (**[5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_5)**). Alternatively, we may observe that for all     j   {\displaystyle j}  ,      |     α + 1  j   − 1  |  ≥ 1 −    Re ⁡ ( α ) + 1  j   ≥ 1   {\textstyle \left|{\frac {\alpha +1}{j}}-1\right|\geq 1-{\frac {\operatorname {Re} (\alpha )+1}{j}}\geq 1}  . Thus, by formula (**[6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_6)**), for all     k ,  |    (   α k   )    |  ≥ 1   {\textstyle k,\left|{\alpha \choose k}\right|\geq 1}  . This completes the proof of (iii). Turning to (iv), we use identity (**[7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_7)**) above with     x = − 1   {\displaystyle x=-1}   and     α − 1   {\displaystyle \alpha -1}   in place of     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  , along with formula (**[4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_4)**), to obtain

      ∑  k = 0   n       (   α k   )    ( − 1  )  k   =     (    α − 1  n   )    ( − 1  )  n   =   1  Γ ( − α + 1 )  n  α      ( 1 + o ( 1 ) )   {\displaystyle \sum _{k=0}^{n}\!{\alpha \choose k}(-1)^{k}=\!{\alpha -1 \choose n}(-1)^{n}={\frac {1}{\Gamma (-\alpha +1)n^{\alpha }}}(1+o(1))}

as     n → ∞   {\displaystyle n\to \infty }  . Assertion (iv) now follows from the asymptotic behavior of the sequence      n  − α   =  e  − α log ⁡ ( n )     {\displaystyle n^{-\alpha }=e^{-\alpha \log(n)}}  . (Precisely,      |  e  − α log ⁡ n   |  =  e  − Re ⁡ ( α ) log ⁡ n     {\displaystyle \left|e^{-\alpha \log n}\right|=e^{-\operatorname {Re} (\alpha )\log n}}   certainly converges to     0   {\displaystyle 0}   if     Re ⁡ ( α ) > 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )>0}   and diverges to     + ∞   {\displaystyle +\infty }   if     Re ⁡ ( α ) < 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )<0}  . If     Re ⁡ ( α ) = 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )=0}  , then      n  − α   =  e  − i Im ⁡ ( α ) log ⁡ n     {\displaystyle n^{-\alpha }=e^{-i\operatorname {Im} (\alpha )\log n}}   converges if and only if the sequence     Im ⁡ ( α ) log ⁡ n   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Im} (\alpha )\log n}   converges      mod  2 π     {\displaystyle {\bmod {2\pi }}}  , which is certainly true if     α = 0   {\displaystyle \alpha =0}   but false if     Im ⁡ ( α ) ≠ 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Im} (\alpha )\neq 0}  : in the latter case the sequence is dense       mod  2 π     {\displaystyle \!{\bmod {2\pi }}}  , due to the fact that     log ⁡ n   {\displaystyle \log n}   diverges and     log ⁡ ( n + 1 ) − log ⁡ n   {\displaystyle \log(n+1)-\log n}   converges to zero).

## Summation of the binomial series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=5)]

The usual argument to compute the sum of the binomial series goes as follows. [Differentiating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative) term-wise the binomial series within the disk of convergence |*x*| < 1 and using formula (**[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_1)**), one has that the sum of the series is an [analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function) solving the [ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation) (1 + *x*)*u*′(*x*) − *αu*(*x*) = 0 with [initial condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_condition) *u*(0) = 1.

The unique solution of this problem is the function *u*(*x*) = (1 + *x*)*α*. Indeed, multiplying by the [integrating factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrating_factor) (1 + *x*)−*α*−1 gives

     0 = ( 1 + x  )  − α    u ′  ( x ) − α ( 1 + x  )  − α − 1   u ( x ) =   [   ( 1 + x  )  − α   u ( x )    ]   ′   ,   {\displaystyle 0=(1+x)^{-\alpha }u'(x)-\alpha (1+x)^{-\alpha -1}u(x)={\big [}(1+x)^{-\alpha }u(x){\big ]}'\,,}

so the function (1 + *x*)*−α**u*(*x*) is a constant, which the initial condition tells us is 1. That is, *u*(*x*) = (1 + *x*)*α* is the sum of the binomial series for |*x*| < 1.

The equality extends to |*x*| = 1 whenever the series converges, as a consequence of [Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel's_theorem) and by [continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function) of (1 + *x*)*α*.

## Negative binomial series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=6)]

Closely related is the *negative binomial series* defined by the [MacLaurin series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacLaurin_series) for the function     g ( x ) = ( 1 − x  )  − α     {\displaystyle g(x)=(1-x)^{-\alpha }}  , where     α ∈  C    {\displaystyle \alpha \in \mathbb {C} }   and      |  x  |  < 1   {\displaystyle |x|<1}  . Explicitly,

           1  ( 1 − x  )  α         =  ∑  k = 0   ∞        g  ( k )   ( 0 )   k !      x  k         = 1 + α x +    α ( α + 1 )   2 !     x  2   +    α ( α + 1 ) ( α + 2 )   3 !     x  3   + ⋯ ,       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}{\frac {1}{(1-x)^{\alpha }}}&=\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }\;{\frac {g^{(k)}(0)}{k!}}\;x^{k}\\&=1+\alpha x+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha +1)}{2!}}x^{2}+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha +1)(\alpha +2)}{3!}}x^{3}+\cdots ,\end{aligned}}}

which is written in terms of the [multiset coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiset_coefficient)

      (       (   α k   )       )  =    (    α + k − 1  k   )    =    α ( α + 1 ) ( α + 2 ) ⋯ ( α + k − 1 )   k !     .   {\displaystyle \left(\!\!{\alpha \choose k}\!\!\right)={\alpha +k-1 \choose k}={\frac {\alpha (\alpha +1)(\alpha +2)\cdots (\alpha +k-1)}{k!}}\,.}

When α is a positive integer, several common sequences are apparent. The case *α* = 1 gives the series 1 + *x* + *x*2 + *x*3 + ..., where the coefficient of each term of the series is simply 1. The case *α* = 2 gives the series 1 + 2*x* + 3*x*2 + 4*x*3 + ..., which has the counting numbers as coefficients. The case *α* = 3 gives the series 1 + 3*x* + 6*x*2 + 10*x*3 + ..., which has the [triangle numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_numbers) as coefficients. The case *α* = 4 gives the series 1 + 4*x* + 10*x*2 + 20*x*3 + ..., which has the [tetrahedral numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedral_numbers) as coefficients, and similarly for higher integer values of α.

The negative binomial series includes the case of the [geometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_series), the [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-1)       1  1 − x    =  ∑  n = 0   ∞    x  n     {\displaystyle {\frac {1}{1-x}}=\sum _{n=0}^{\infty }x^{n}}   (which is the negative binomial series when     α = 1   {\displaystyle \alpha =1}  , convergent in the disc      |  x  |  < 1   {\displaystyle |x|<1}  ) and, more generally, series obtained by differentiation of the geometric power series:       1  ( 1 − x  )  n      =   1  ( n − 1 ) !       d  n − 1    d  x  n − 1        1  1 − x      {\displaystyle {\frac {1}{(1-x)^{n}}}={\frac {1}{(n-1)!}}{\frac {d^{n-1}}{dx^{n-1}}}{\frac {1}{1-x}}}   with     α = n   {\displaystyle \alpha =n}  , a positive integer.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=7)]

The first results concerning binomial series for other than positive-integer exponents were given by Sir [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton) in the study of [areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) enclosed under certain curves. [John Wallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wallis) built upon this work by considering expressions of the form *y* = (1 − *x*2)*m* where m is a fraction. He found that (written in modern terms) the successive coefficients *c**k* of (−*x*2)*k* are to be found by multiplying the preceding coefficient by ⁠m − (k − 1)/k⁠ (as in the case of integer exponents), thereby implicitly giving a formula for these coefficients. He explicitly writes the following instances[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-4)

     ( 1 −  x  2    )  1  /  2   = 1 −    x  2   2   −    x  4   8   −    x  6   16   ⋯   {\displaystyle (1-x^{2})^{1/2}=1-{\frac {x^{2}}{2}}-{\frac {x^{4}}{8}}-{\frac {x^{6}}{16}}\cdots }       ( 1 −  x  2    )  3  /  2   = 1 −    3  x  2    2   +    3  x  4    8   +    x  6   16   ⋯   {\displaystyle (1-x^{2})^{3/2}=1-{\frac {3x^{2}}{2}}+{\frac {3x^{4}}{8}}+{\frac {x^{6}}{16}}\cdots }       ( 1 −  x  2    )  1  /  3   = 1 −    x  2   3   −    x  4   9   −    5  x  6    81   ⋯   {\displaystyle (1-x^{2})^{1/3}=1-{\frac {x^{2}}{3}}-{\frac {x^{4}}{9}}-{\frac {5x^{6}}{81}}\cdots }

The binomial series is therefore sometimes referred to as [Newton's binomial theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_theorem#Newton's_generalized_binomial_theorem). Newton gives no proof and is not explicit about the nature of the series. Later, on 1826 [Niels Henrik Abel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels_Henrik_Abel) discussed the subject in a paper published on *[Crelle's Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crelle's_Journal)*, treating notably questions of convergence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbel1826-5)

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q833480#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Mathematical series

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), the **binomial series** is a generalization of the [binomial formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_formula) to cases where the [exponent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponent) is not a positive integer:

         ( 1 + x  )  α      =  ∑  k = 0   ∞       (   α k   )     x  k         = 1 + α x +    α ( α − 1 )   2 !     x  2   +    α ( α − 1 ) ( α − 2 )   3 !     x  3   + ⋯       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}(1+x)^{\alpha }&=\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }\!{\binom {\alpha }{k}}x^{k}\\&=1+\alpha x+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha -1)}{2!}}x^{2}+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha -1)(\alpha -2)}{3!}}x^{3}+\cdots \end{aligned}}}    1

where     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   is any [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number), and the [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series) on the right-hand side is expressed in terms of the [(generalized) binomial coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient#Generalization_and_connection_to_the_binomial_series)

        (   α k   )    =    α ( α − 1 ) ( α − 2 ) ⋯ ( α − k + 1 )   k !    .   {\displaystyle {\binom {\alpha }{k}}={\frac {\alpha (\alpha -1)(\alpha -2)\cdots (\alpha -k+1)}{k!}}.}

The binomial series is the [MacLaurin series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacLaurin_series) for the [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics))     f ( x ) = ( 1 + x  )  α     {\displaystyle f(x)=(1+x)^{\alpha }}  . It converges when      |  x  |  < 1   {\displaystyle |x|<1}  .

If α is a nonnegative [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) n then the *x**n* + 1 term and all later terms in the series are 0, since each contains a factor of (*n* − *n*). In this case, the series is a finite polynomial, equivalent to the binomial formula.

Convergence

# Convergence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=1)]

Conditions for convergence

# Conditions for convergence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=2)]

Whether (**[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_1)**) [converges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_series) depends on the values of the complex numbers α and x. More precisely:

1. If |*x*| < 1, the series converges [absolutely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_convergence) for any complex number α.
2. If |*x*| = 1, the series converges absolutely [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) either Re(*α*) > 0 or *α* = 0, where Re(*α*) denotes the [real part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) of α.
3. If |*x*| = 1 and *x* ≠ −1, the series converges if and only if Re(*α*) > −1.
4. If *x* = −1, the series converges if and only if either Re(*α*) > 0 or *α* = 0.
5. If |*x*| > 1, the series [diverges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_series) except when α is a non-negative integer, in which case the series is a finite sum.

In particular, if α is not a non-negative integer, the situation at the boundary of the [disk of convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_of_convergence), |*x*| = 1, is summarized as follows:

- If Re(*α*) > 0, the series converges absolutely.
- If −1 < Re(*α*) ≤ 0, the series converges [conditionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_convergence) if *x* ≠ −1 and diverges if *x* = −1.
- If Re(*α*) ≤ −1, the series diverges.

Identities to be used in the proof

# Identities to be used in the proof

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=3)]

The following hold for any complex number α:

        (   α 0   )     = 1 ,   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose 0}\!=1,}          (   α  k + 1    )     =     (   α k   )       α − k   k + 1    ,   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k+1}\!=\!{\alpha \choose k}{\frac {\alpha -k}{k+1}},}    2        (   α  k − 1    )     +     (   α k   )     =     (    α + 1  k   )    .   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k-1}\!+\!{\alpha \choose k}\!=\!{\alpha +1 \choose k}.}    3

Unless     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   is a nonnegative integer (in which case the binomial coefficients vanish as     k   {\displaystyle k}   is larger than     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  ), a useful [asymptotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_analysis) relationship for the binomial coefficients is, in [Landau notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_notation):

        (   α k   )     =    ( − 1  )  k     Γ ( − α )  k  1 + α       ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) ,   as   k → ∞ .   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k}\!={\frac {(-1)^{k}}{\Gamma (-\alpha )k^{1+\alpha }}}\,(1+o(1)),\quad {\text{as }}k\to \infty .}    4

This is essentially equivalent to Euler's definition of the [Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function):

     Γ ( z ) =  lim  k → ∞      k !   k  z     z ( z + 1 ) ⋯ ( z + k )    ,   {\displaystyle \Gamma (z)=\lim _{k\to \infty }{\frac {k!\,k^{z}}{z(z+1)\cdots (z+k)}},}

and implies immediately the coarser bounds

       m  k  1 + Re  α     ≤  |    (   α k   )    |  ≤   M  k  1 + Re ⁡ α     ,   {\displaystyle {\frac {m}{k^{1+\operatorname {Re} \,\alpha }}}\leq \left|{\alpha \choose k}\right|\leq {\frac {M}{k^{1+\operatorname {Re} \alpha }}},}    5

for some positive constants m and M .

Formula (**[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_2)**) for the generalized binomial coefficient can be rewritten as

        (   α k   )     =  ∏  j = 1   k     (     α + 1  j   − 1  )  .   {\displaystyle {\alpha \choose k}\!=\prod _{j=1}^{k}\!\left({\frac {\alpha +1}{j}}-1\right).}    6

Proof

# Proof

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=4)]

To prove (i) and (v), apply the [ratio test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio_test) and use formula (**[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_2)**) above to show that whenever     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   is not a nonnegative integer, the [radius of convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_of_convergence) is exactly 1. Part (ii) follows from formula (**[5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_5)**), by comparison with the [p-series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_tests#p-series_test)

      ∑  k = 1   ∞     1  k  p     ,   {\displaystyle \sum _{k=1}^{\infty }{\frac {1}{k^{p}}},}

with     p = 1 + Re ⁡ ( α )   {\displaystyle p=1+\operatorname {Re} (\alpha )}  . To prove (iii), first use formula (**[3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_3)**) to obtain

     ( 1 + x )  ∑  k = 0   n       (   α k   )     x  k   =  ∑  k = 0   n       (    α + 1  k   )     x  k   +    (   α n   )     x  n + 1   ,   {\displaystyle (1+x)\sum _{k=0}^{n}\!{\alpha \choose k}x^{k}=\sum _{k=0}^{n}\!{\alpha +1 \choose k}x^{k}+{\alpha \choose n}x^{n+1},}    7

and then use (ii) and formula (**[5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_5)**) again to prove convergence of the right-hand side when     Re ⁡ ( α ) > − 1   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )>-1}   is assumed. On the other hand, the series does not converge if      |  x  |  = 1   {\displaystyle |x|=1}   and     Re ⁡ ( α ) ≤ − 1   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )\leq -1}  , again by formula (**[5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_5)**). Alternatively, we may observe that for all     j   {\displaystyle j}  ,      |     α + 1  j   − 1  |  ≥ 1 −    Re ⁡ ( α ) + 1  j   ≥ 1   {\textstyle \left|{\frac {\alpha +1}{j}}-1\right|\geq 1-{\frac {\operatorname {Re} (\alpha )+1}{j}}\geq 1}  . Thus, by formula (**[6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_6)**), for all     k ,  |    (   α k   )    |  ≥ 1   {\textstyle k,\left|{\alpha \choose k}\right|\geq 1}  . This completes the proof of (iii). Turning to (iv), we use identity (**[7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_7)**) above with     x = − 1   {\displaystyle x=-1}   and     α − 1   {\displaystyle \alpha -1}   in place of     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }  , along with formula (**[4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_4)**), to obtain

      ∑  k = 0   n       (   α k   )    ( − 1  )  k   =     (    α − 1  n   )    ( − 1  )  n   =   1  Γ ( − α + 1 )  n  α      ( 1 + o ( 1 ) )   {\displaystyle \sum _{k=0}^{n}\!{\alpha \choose k}(-1)^{k}=\!{\alpha -1 \choose n}(-1)^{n}={\frac {1}{\Gamma (-\alpha +1)n^{\alpha }}}(1+o(1))}

as     n → ∞   {\displaystyle n\to \infty }  . Assertion (iv) now follows from the asymptotic behavior of the sequence      n  − α   =  e  − α log ⁡ ( n )     {\displaystyle n^{-\alpha }=e^{-\alpha \log(n)}}  . (Precisely,      |  e  − α log ⁡ n   |  =  e  − Re ⁡ ( α ) log ⁡ n     {\displaystyle \left|e^{-\alpha \log n}\right|=e^{-\operatorname {Re} (\alpha )\log n}}   certainly converges to     0   {\displaystyle 0}   if     Re ⁡ ( α ) > 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )>0}   and diverges to     + ∞   {\displaystyle +\infty }   if     Re ⁡ ( α ) < 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )<0}  . If     Re ⁡ ( α ) = 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Re} (\alpha )=0}  , then      n  − α   =  e  − i Im ⁡ ( α ) log ⁡ n     {\displaystyle n^{-\alpha }=e^{-i\operatorname {Im} (\alpha )\log n}}   converges if and only if the sequence     Im ⁡ ( α ) log ⁡ n   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Im} (\alpha )\log n}   converges      mod  2 π     {\displaystyle {\bmod {2\pi }}}  , which is certainly true if     α = 0   {\displaystyle \alpha =0}   but false if     Im ⁡ ( α ) ≠ 0   {\displaystyle \operatorname {Im} (\alpha )\neq 0}  : in the latter case the sequence is dense       mod  2 π     {\displaystyle \!{\bmod {2\pi }}}  , due to the fact that     log ⁡ n   {\displaystyle \log n}   diverges and     log ⁡ ( n + 1 ) − log ⁡ n   {\displaystyle \log(n+1)-\log n}   converges to zero).

Summation of the binomial series

# Summation of the binomial series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=5)]

The usual argument to compute the sum of the binomial series goes as follows. [Differentiating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative) term-wise the binomial series within the disk of convergence |*x*| < 1 and using formula (**[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#math_1)**), one has that the sum of the series is an [analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function) solving the [ordinary differential equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation) (1 + *x*)*u*′(*x*) − *αu*(*x*) = 0 with [initial condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_condition) *u*(0) = 1.

The unique solution of this problem is the function *u*(*x*) = (1 + *x*)*α*. Indeed, multiplying by the [integrating factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrating_factor) (1 + *x*)−*α*−1 gives

     0 = ( 1 + x  )  − α    u ′  ( x ) − α ( 1 + x  )  − α − 1   u ( x ) =   [   ( 1 + x  )  − α   u ( x )    ]   ′   ,   {\displaystyle 0=(1+x)^{-\alpha }u'(x)-\alpha (1+x)^{-\alpha -1}u(x)={\big [}(1+x)^{-\alpha }u(x){\big ]}'\,,}

so the function (1 + *x*)*−α**u*(*x*) is a constant, which the initial condition tells us is 1. That is, *u*(*x*) = (1 + *x*)*α* is the sum of the binomial series for |*x*| < 1.

The equality extends to |*x*| = 1 whenever the series converges, as a consequence of [Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel's_theorem) and by [continuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function) of (1 + *x*)*α*.

Negative binomial series

# Negative binomial series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=6)]

Closely related is the *negative binomial series* defined by the [MacLaurin series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacLaurin_series) for the function     g ( x ) = ( 1 − x  )  − α     {\displaystyle g(x)=(1-x)^{-\alpha }}  , where     α ∈  C    {\displaystyle \alpha \in \mathbb {C} }   and      |  x  |  < 1   {\displaystyle |x|<1}  . Explicitly,

           1  ( 1 − x  )  α         =  ∑  k = 0   ∞        g  ( k )   ( 0 )   k !      x  k         = 1 + α x +    α ( α + 1 )   2 !     x  2   +    α ( α + 1 ) ( α + 2 )   3 !     x  3   + ⋯ ,       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}{\frac {1}{(1-x)^{\alpha }}}&=\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }\;{\frac {g^{(k)}(0)}{k!}}\;x^{k}\\&=1+\alpha x+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha +1)}{2!}}x^{2}+{\frac {\alpha (\alpha +1)(\alpha +2)}{3!}}x^{3}+\cdots ,\end{aligned}}}

which is written in terms of the [multiset coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiset_coefficient)

      (       (   α k   )       )  =    (    α + k − 1  k   )    =    α ( α + 1 ) ( α + 2 ) ⋯ ( α + k − 1 )   k !     .   {\displaystyle \left(\!\!{\alpha \choose k}\!\!\right)={\alpha +k-1 \choose k}={\frac {\alpha (\alpha +1)(\alpha +2)\cdots (\alpha +k-1)}{k!}}\,.}

When α is a positive integer, several common sequences are apparent. The case *α* = 1 gives the series 1 + *x* + *x*2 + *x*3 + ..., where the coefficient of each term of the series is simply 1. The case *α* = 2 gives the series 1 + 2*x* + 3*x*2 + 4*x*3 + ..., which has the counting numbers as coefficients. The case *α* = 3 gives the series 1 + 3*x* + 6*x*2 + 10*x*3 + ..., which has the [triangle numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_numbers) as coefficients. The case *α* = 4 gives the series 1 + 4*x* + 10*x*2 + 20*x*3 + ..., which has the [tetrahedral numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedral_numbers) as coefficients, and similarly for higher integer values of α.

The negative binomial series includes the case of the [geometric series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_series), the [power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-1)       1  1 − x    =  ∑  n = 0   ∞    x  n     {\displaystyle {\frac {1}{1-x}}=\sum _{n=0}^{\infty }x^{n}}   (which is the negative binomial series when     α = 1   {\displaystyle \alpha =1}  , convergent in the disc      |  x  |  < 1   {\displaystyle |x|<1}  ) and, more generally, series obtained by differentiation of the geometric power series:       1  ( 1 − x  )  n      =   1  ( n − 1 ) !       d  n − 1    d  x  n − 1        1  1 − x      {\displaystyle {\frac {1}{(1-x)^{n}}}={\frac {1}{(n-1)!}}{\frac {d^{n-1}}{dx^{n-1}}}{\frac {1}{1-x}}}   with     α = n   {\displaystyle \alpha =n}  , a positive integer.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-2)

History

# History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Binomial_series&action=edit&section=7)]

The first results concerning binomial series for other than positive-integer exponents were given by Sir [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton) in the study of [areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) enclosed under certain curves. [John Wallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wallis) built upon this work by considering expressions of the form *y* = (1 − *x*2)*m* where m is a fraction. He found that (written in modern terms) the successive coefficients *c**k* of (−*x*2)*k* are to be found by multiplying the preceding coefficient by ⁠m − (k − 1)/k⁠ (as in the case of integer exponents), thereby implicitly giving a formula for these coefficients. He explicitly writes the following instances[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-4)

     ( 1 −  x  2    )  1  /  2   = 1 −    x  2   2   −    x  4   8   −    x  6   16   ⋯   {\displaystyle (1-x^{2})^{1/2}=1-{\frac {x^{2}}{2}}-{\frac {x^{4}}{8}}-{\frac {x^{6}}{16}}\cdots }       ( 1 −  x  2    )  3  /  2   = 1 −    3  x  2    2   +    3  x  4    8   +    x  6   16   ⋯   {\displaystyle (1-x^{2})^{3/2}=1-{\frac {3x^{2}}{2}}+{\frac {3x^{4}}{8}}+{\frac {x^{6}}{16}}\cdots }       ( 1 −  x  2    )  1  /  3   = 1 −    x  2   3   −    x  4   9   −    5  x  6    81   ⋯   {\displaystyle (1-x^{2})^{1/3}=1-{\frac {x^{2}}{3}}-{\frac {x^{4}}{9}}-{\frac {5x^{6}}{81}}\cdots }

The binomial series is therefore sometimes referred to as [Newton's binomial theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_theorem#Newton's_generalized_binomial_theorem). Newton gives no proof and is not explicit about the nature of the series. Later, on 1826 [Niels Henrik Abel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels_Henrik_Abel) discussed the subject in a paper published on *[Crelle's Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crelle's_Journal)*, treating notably questions of convergence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_series#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbel1826-5)
